div.head: EGu Prol.
div.ab: And þis is seo gerædnis eac, þe Ælfred cẏng ⁊ Guðrum cyng ⁊ eft Eadward cyng (⁊ Guðrum cyng) gecuran ⁊ gecwædon, þa þa Engle ⁊ Dene to friþe ⁊ to freondscipe fullice fengon; ⁊ þa witan eac, þe syððan wæron, oft ⁊ unseldan þæt seolfe geniwodon ⁊ mid gode gehihtan.

And ðis is seo gerædnyss eac, ðe Ælfred cyng ⁊ Guðrum cyng ⁊ eft Eadward cyng (⁊ Gyþrum cyng) gecuran ⁊ gecwædon, ða ða Engle ⁊ Dene to friðe ⁊ to freondscipe fullice fengon; ⁊ ða witan eac, ðe syððan wæron, oft ⁊ unseldan þæt seolfe geniwodon ⁊ mid gode gehuhtan.

Hoc est consilium, quod Ælfred rex et Godrún rex elegerunt et (con)dixerunt, quando Angli et Dani ad pacem et amicitiam (ad concordiam) plene conuenerunt; et sapientes etiam, qui postea fuerunt (successerunt), sepius hoc et assidue (nobis) renouauerunt et in bonum (semper) adauxerunt.

And þis is seo gerædnis eac, þe Ælfred cyng ⁊ Guðrum cyng ⁊ eft Eadward cyng (⁊ Guðrum cyng) gecuran ⁊ gecwædon, þa þa Engle ⁊ Dene to friþe ⁊ to freondscipe fullice fengon; ⁊ þa witan eac, þe syððan wæron, oft ⁊ unseldan þæt seolfe geniwodon ⁊ mid gode geiehtan.

And þis is seo gerædnis eac þe Ælfred cyng and Guðrum cyng, and eft Eadward cyng and Guðrum cyng, gecuran and gecwædon þa þa Engle and Dene to friþe and to freondscipe fullice fengon. And þa witan eac, þe syððan wæron, oft and unseldan þæt seolfe geniwodon and mid gode gehihtan.

Und dies ist ferner die Satzung, welche König Aelfred und König Guthrum (und späterhin König Eadward und König Guthrum fehlt Quadr.) erkoren und bestimmten, damals als Engländer und Dänen Friede und Freundschaft völlig anfingen; und die Witan auch, die später waren, erneuten oft und nicht selten dasselbe und vermehrten [es] mit Gutem.

And this is further the ordinance which King Alfred and King Guthrum (and later King Edward and King Guthrum lacking in Quadr.) chose and determined at the time when the English and the Danes fully entered into peace and friendship; and the councillors also, who came later, often and not seldom renewed the same and increased [it] with good things.

This also is the legislation which King Alfred and King Guthrum, and afterwards King Edward and King Guthrum, enacted and agreed upon, when the English and the Danes unreservedly entered into relations of peace and friendship. The councillors also who have been [in office] since then, frequently and often have re-enacted the same, and added improvements thereto.

And this also is the decree which King Alfred and King Guthrum, and later King Edward and King Guthrum, agreed upon and proclaimed when the English and the Danes fully resolved on peace and friendship. And also the councilors, those who came after, often and frequently renewed it and strengthened it with improvements.

And this also: The opening phrase appears to connect this text with the one immediately preceding it in the manuscript, the so-called Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum, composed sometime after King Alfred of Wessex (849–899) defeated the Viking king Guthrum (d. 890) at the battle of Ethandun (identified as Edington in Wiltshire) in May 878. It seems likely that Wulfstan composed The Laws of Edward and Guthrum as a companion piece to the Treaty—possibly as a way of extending the provisions of the earlier treaty to encompass northern England as well as southern—and intended the two to circulate together.

Den Vertrag schliesst also der Gesamtstaat England, nicht ‘Angeln’ [Ostangliens], mit Nordleuten, laut des Vorhergehenden nur denen des Einen Kleinstaats von Ostanglien. Auch in I Cn Insc. D wird die Gesetzgebung an solchen Vertrag zwischen den eingeborenen Engländern und den Nordischen Siegern geknüpft, in Worten, die an EGu anklingen

The treaty, then, is concluded by the whole state of England, not by the ‘Angles’ [of East Anglia], with Northmen — according to what precedes, only those of the one small kingdom of East Anglia. In I Cn Insc. D too the legislation is linked to such a treaty between the native English and the Northern conquerors, in words that echo EGu
Vgl. Gl altes Recht; Gesetz 23; o. Einl. 19
Cf. Gl altes Recht; Gesetz 23; above Introduction 19

The fact that no king is mentioned here or in cap. 4, 5 § 1, may indicate, as Liebermann suggests, that the laws were enacted at a provincial (East Anglian) assembly (cf. III As. Preamble), after the kingdom had ceased to exist. On the other hand, reference may be made to IV As. Preamble, where the laws are attributed to the action of a council, though the king is mentioned. We may also compare the Preamble to the Laws of Wihtred.
